title: What kind of mark is the crease of a folded paper?
description: A sheet of paper is folded and opened out, and a finger runs along the crease from one edge to the other. Two dots mark where the crease starts and where it stops. Keeko's doubt, that a straight crease goes on forever, is broken by the two edges where the crease stops.
teaching_notes: One idea: a straight piece with two end points is a line segment. Watch for students who think that a straight mark must go on forever.

source: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (T
video_script.why: The child sees that the crease of a folded paper is a straight mark with two end points, which is the first picture of a line segment.
video_script.substitution: Treat the crease as a straight pencil mark with a dot at each end.
video_script.anchor: a sheet of paper folded and opened out again, with the crease running from one edge to the other
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the crease goes on forever because it is straight. The opened paper shows the crease stops at two edges, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The crease is a line segment with end points eigh and B

final_answer.value: Yes; the crease is a line segment with end points A and B
final_answer.spoken: yes, the crease is a line segment with end points eigh and B

never_show: the word line segment before the answer beat
maths_rules: A fold in paper leaves a crease, and the crease is a straight mark.
The crease begins at one edge of the paper, at point A, and stops at the other edge, at point B.
A straight piece with two end points is a line segment, so the crease is the line segment AB.
Slip: a straight mark does not have to go on forever; this one stops at A and at B.
video_script.design: One idea: straight, with two end points, is a line segment. The same sheet of paper stays for the whole video. The wrong idea is that a straight mark goes on forever.
